operation_tail.detail: OS Open UPRN supplies coordinate references associated with UPRNs for addressable locations across Great Britain; it is not treated as a UK-wide Northern Ireland address source.
A UPRN is treated as the unique numeric identifier for an addressable location and remains distinct from postcode, parcel and provider identifiers.
The product overview describes approximately 40 million addressable locations; this is product-scale context, not a parcel count.
Residential properties are within the addressable-location universe represented by UPRNs.
Commercial properties are also included, so residential and business scopes must not be inferred from UPRN presence alone.
Objects without normal postal addresses, including examples such as bus shelters and electricity substations, may have UPRNs.
UPRNs are primarily allocated by local authorities under their maintenance duties, preserving authoritative identifier provenance.
The technical schema allows UPRNs assigned by an LLPG custodian or Ordnance Survey; allocation source is not guessed from the number.
A UPRN is retained as a persistent identifier for the addressable location even when descriptive address information changes.
The official documentation states that a UPRN is never reused, so historical associations remain bound to the original location identity.
A property-name change does not create a replacement UPRN solely because the address text changed.
A change in property use does not by itself change the persistent UPRN.
Demolished locations remain represented by their UPRN, preventing demolition-state records from being mistaken for live service premises.
OS Open UPRN is synchronised with AddressBase Premium for completeness and currency.
The product includes UPRNs independently of lifecycle state, so UPRN presence alone is not evidence that a premise is active.
Under-construction UPRNs are explicitly included and cannot be promoted to current occupied-service status.
In-use UPRNs are included, but the open product does not itself expose the lifecycle classification needed to select only these records.
Demolished UPRNs are included in the open coordinate product and require external lifecycle evidence before service matching.
The dataset contains the position of each included AddressBase Premium record together with its UPRN.
Datasets may be linked using the UPRN when both sources carry the same authoritative identifier.
Spatial association by address-point position is supported, but proximity matching is not treated as equivalent to an exact UPRN join.
The product is designed for use in GIS applications.
The product can be integrated into a spatial database without converting point identifiers into parcel polygons.
OS Open UPRN is a vector identifier dataset rather than raster coverage or measured network-performance data.
The downloadable product is available in CSV format.
The downloadable product is also available as an OGC GeoPackage.
The technical specification defines one OS Open UPRN feature type, simplifying schema validation.
FID is present only in the GeoPackage representation.
FID is autogenerated and non-persistent, so it is never substituted for UPRN.
The UPRN attribute is specified as an integer with size 12 and mandatory multiplicity one.
X_COORDINATE is expressed in British National Grid metres with documented precision and scale of 8,2.
Y_COORDINATE is expressed in British National Grid metres with documented precision and scale of 9,2.
LATITUDE is provided in ETRS89 with documented precision and scale of 9,7.
LONGITUDE is provided in ETRS89 with documented precision and scale of 8,7.
GeoPackage records are supplied as point geometry representing the address-record location.
An address point is not promoted to a cadastral parcel polygon or building footprint.
GeoPackage geometry is supplied in BNG using the X and Y coordinate attributes, enabling consistency checks.
Both CSV and GeoPackage representations expose the five core fields UPRN, X_COORDINATE, Y_COORDINATE, LATITUDE and LONGITUDE.
The open product's core schema does not provide full address text, postcode, classification or lifecycle fields.
CSV supply is one file for the whole of Great Britain containing all records.
The CSV contains column headers and ingestion validates them before reading records.
The CSV supply contract states one record per line.
CSV fields are comma-separated.
Rows are not expected to end with a trailing comma.
CSV records are documented as terminated by carriage return and line feed.
GeoPackage supply is one file for the whole of Great Britain.
The product is supplied as a free online download without registration through the OS Data Hub.
Both formats are supplied as full datasets only.
Area-of-interest orders are not available for OS Open UPRN.
Change-Only Updates are not available; refreshes require a new full-supply reconciliation.
The product refreshes every six weeks in line with AddressBase Premium epoch dates.
Each downloaded snapshot must retain its publication epoch and source currency rather than being labelled only as current.
The official known-issues page listed no live OS Open UPRN issue at review time; this is a dated page observation, not a permanent guarantee.
Participating providers should supply speed information during purchase without the customer having to request it.
Residential estimated speeds are tied to the 8-10pm busy-time window.
Business estimated speeds are tied to the 12-2pm busy-time window.
A busy-time estimate is kept separate from headline maximum or technology capability.
The provider should give a personalised minimum guaranteed speed for the purchased service.
For superfast products, the guarantee may use the capability of the line entering the specific home or office.
A personalised pre-contract speed figure is still an estimate and is not stored as a measured parcel result.
Ofcom recommends an Ethernet-connected computer or tablet for the most accurate practical speed test.
Wi-Fi can slow the signal, so wireless test results are not treated as access-line performance without qualification.
The contract or provider remains the source for the speed the customer should be receiving.
Customers are directed to the provider to diagnose an apparent speed problem.
The code's remedy depends on the unresolved problem lying within the provider's network.
A participating provider that cannot fix an in-network problem within 30 days must offer the applicable exit right.
The exit remedy is without an early termination charge when the code conditions are met.
The exit right can extend to products linked financially, contractually or technically to the broadband service.
The code's 30-day exit process does not apply in the same way to rolling monthly contracts.
After purchase, speed estimates and relevant speed-affecting policies should be supplied in a durable written or account form.
Policies that may affect speed are recorded separately from network-availability evidence.
Automatic compensation for delayed start or missed appointments is not treated as proof of speed or coverage.
Advertising-speed claims use the average received by at least 50% of customers at the busiest time, distinct from an individual guarantee.
Business-code signatories provide expected download access-line estimates before the customer commits.
Expected upload access-line estimates are also supplied before commitment.
Throughput estimates are supplied where available and remain distinct from access-line speed.
Relevant business speed information is provided in writing after sale.
Business-code signatories must manage speed problems and assist customers in resolving them.
A business customer may exit without penalty when download speed remains below the minimum guarantee after an opportunity to resolve it.
The business code applies regardless of business size for covered services.
The business code describes standard services across ADSL, cable, FTTC, FTTP, wireless and satellite.
Some line-speed and exit provisions are technology-specific and cannot be applied uniformly.
Certain provisions do not apply to FTTP and cable in the same way because their performance is described as less variable.
Services with guaranteed speeds or dedicated connections fall outside the standard business code scope.
Consumer and business speed-code protections are not promoted to postcode or premise availability evidence.
